source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsacker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: LLMs were tested on chess positions graded by familiarity: common opening positions (within-distribution, WD), random-play positions (near, ND), and random piece placement (out-of-distribution, OOD). Move quality falls steeply as positions get less familiar, and base models drop to random-move level on random placement. This is the nearest LLM analogue of the Chase-Simon game versus random board contrast.
numbers: N=500 positions per condition (1,500 total). WD = at least 1,000 occurrences in Lichess Masters; ND = 10 random moves per side; OOD = 10 pieces per side placed at random. GPT-5 on WD: centipawn loss 26.19 (SD 49.53), better than random; on OOD no base model beats random.
limits: Observational, no randomized manipulation of training data. Random placement also changes tactics, not only familiarity. No human baseline on the same positions (authors say so).
agent_relevance: LLM skill is tied to familiar patterns, as chunking theory says for humans. Expect a sharp drop on unfamiliar inputs and do not trust fluent output there.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsacker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Illegal-move rate rises sharply as positions get less familiar, although the rules of legality are identical everywhere. The authors call this their most robust evidence of failed generalization.
numbers: Illegal moves on OOD: GPT-3.5 74.7%, GPT-4o 41.6%, GPT-5 33.8%. Claude Opus: WD ACPL 14.0, illegal 0.2%; ND ACPL 207.2, illegal 8.2%; OOD ACPL 728.6, illegal 51.6%. Gemini: WD 34.8 / 2.2%; ND 434.1 / 17.0%; OOD 829.7 / 72.0%.
limits: Syntax errors were 14.4% for Claude Opus versus under 1% for most others, so format problems may add to the figures. Reasoning-augmented GPT-5 still above 10% illegal on OOD.
agent_relevance: Rule checks must run in code, because a model can lose even bounded rule application when input is unfamiliar. A legality check is cheap and catches the failure.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsacker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Extra reasoning tokens help, but least where priors are sparse. Reasoning cut centipawn loss by 71.74% overall. Per-token relative marginal gain falls from 22.55% (WD) to 7.23% (ND) and 3.81% (OOD).
numbers: Relative ACPL decrease: ND 85.3%, WD 77.25%, OOD 64.69%. GPT-5 moderate reasoning uses about 5 times as many reasoning tokens on OOD as on WD yet still proposes over 10% illegal moves on OOD.
limits: Single model family for the token analysis; reasoning effort set by the API.
agent_relevance: Spend thinking where checks fail, not evenly (G1, G7). Return on thinking is lowest where the agent lacks relevant experience, so retrieval of precedent matters more there than more tokens.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsacker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
finding: Newer GPT versions improve, but the improvement slows as positions get less familiar. The paper also states the human counterpoint: human expertise rests on chunking (Chase and Simon 1973), so humans would also be hurt on random boards, but should stay rule-compliant.
numbers: Illegal-move drop GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o 44.31%, then 18.75% GPT-4o to GPT-5. ACPL improvement GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o: 70.7% (WD), 35.16% (ND), 9.08% (OOD); GPT-4o to GPT-5: 69.92%, 10.77%, 5.73%.
limits: The human claim rests on one small cited study, not on this paper's data.
agent_relevance: Scale alone is an unreliable fix for unfamiliar-input failure. Add code-side verification, not trust in the next model release.

source: Reingold and Sheridan (2023) double-check detection with expert and novice chess players, symbol versus letter notation (as reported by Pleiss et al. 2026, appendix C.7)
finding: Experts and novices detected double check with error under 1% in both familiar symbol notation and unfamiliar letter notation. The unfamiliar notation slowed answers but did not lower accuracy.
numbers: Error rate below 1% for both groups in both notations (as quoted in Pleiss et al.).
limits: Not opened; known only through Pleiss et al. Simplified task, not full chess.
agent_relevance: Humans keep rule-following under unfamiliarity at a time cost; LLMs lose legality instead. A scaffold can trade tokens for rule compliance only if a code check enforces it.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models (COLM)
finding: A GPT trained only on next-character prediction of chess game text learns an internal board state (linear probes) and plays strategic chess with no rule knowledge given.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16 layers) and 99.6% (8 layers). Win rate vs Stockfish 16 level 0: 64% (16 layer), 46% (8 layer). Every game in a 100-game sample was unique by move 10.
limits: Small model trained on millions of real games, not a general LLM.
agent_relevance: Pattern-based competence can be learned from data alone and carries an internal state: the machine analogue of chunk-based board perception.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models (COLM)
finding: Randomized boards (20 random opening moves) act like Chase-Simon random positions: the win rate collapses. The model reads such games as low skill (its Elo probe labelled 99.4% of 4,000 random-start games low skill), and adding a skill vector restores much of the ability.
numbers: Win rate vs Stockfish level 0 over 5,000 games: standard board 69.6% (16 layer) and 49.6% (8 layer); random board 16.7% and 15.7%; with positive skill intervention on random board 43.2% and 31.3% (2.6x and 2x).
limits: The explanation (random boards read as weak players) is a hypothesis supported by the probe, not proven. Table win rates differ from the 64% and 46% in the text because of set-up.
agent_relevance: The model infers a latent skill level from context and acts at that level. An expert-context prompt may lift output; this is also why role prompts can change quality.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models (COLM)
finding: Earlier OthelloGPT trained on synthetic uniform random games gave a board state recoverable only by non-linear probes; the chess model trained on real human games had a linear board representation and also learned a skill estimate.
numbers: Best board probe accuracy 99.6%; intervention success up to 92%; legal moves stay above 98% after skill interventions.
limits: One architecture family; chess only.
agent_relevance: Real structured data produces chunk-like structure; random data does less. Favors libraries of real verified cases over synthetic ones.

source: Toshniwal, Wiseman, Livescu, Gimpel (2022) Chess as a Testbed for Language Model State Tracking, AAAI-22
finding: GPT-2 small trained on move strings only can track piece locations and predict legal moves given enough data. Adding random piece-type tokens during training (RAP) improves tracking and lowers perplexity, mainly for small data.
numbers: With the large training set and RAP, legal starting-square accuracy about 100%; drops to 91.3% with the small set. Legal ending squares above 97%; R-precision about 85%.
limits: GPT-2 sized model, not a modern LLM. Value is in the data-scaling shape.
agent_relevance: Representation choice matters: giving the model board-relevant tokens helps. A scaffold can supply a structured state summary instead of raw history.

source: Toshniwal, Wiseman, Livescu, Gimpel (2022) Chess as a Testbed for Language Model State Tracking, AAAI-22
finding: Limiting attention to the last 50 tokens, or using an LSTM, hurts board tracking; full history helps.
numbers: GPT-2 with window 50 is worse than full attention at every data size, especially small and medium. LSTM worse still.
limits: One setting.
agent_relevance: State must be carried; a loop that drops older context without a compact state record loses the board. Keep a code-held state object.

source: Kolasani et al. (2025) LLM CHESS: Benchmarking Reasoning and Instruction-Following in LLMs through Chess
finding: Over 50 models played 30 games each as black against a random-move opponent. Most could not beat a random agent consistently. Reasoning models are far better than non-reasoning ones.
numbers: Reasoning models average win rate 45.4%, top ones near 100%. Instruction-following errors: 71.9% for non-reasoning versus 24.4% for reasoning. Best Elo estimate (o3 low) about 758, far below master level.
limits: Random opponent is weak; the model controls move format so some failures are format, not chess skill.
agent_relevance: Pre-trained domain knowledge is not enough for sustained agent play; verification and format control are needed.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess (searchless chess)
finding: A 270M-parameter transformer trained by supervised learning on Stockfish-labelled Lichess positions plays at grandmaster level with no search. This is recognition-only expertise, the machine form of the de Groot and Chase-Simon claim that expert skill is mostly perception.
numbers: 10 million games, 15.3 billion action-value labels; Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; 10K puzzle test set; only 1.33% of test puzzles overlap training.
limits: Engine labels, not human labels; blitz Elo against online humans and bots; not a general language model.
agent_relevance: A fast pattern policy can match deep search in a narrow domain, but needs huge data. For us, a library of verified examples plus retrieval is the cheap form.

source: Jiao, Eilender, Tang, Anderson (2026) Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels
finding: Maia-2 (predicts human moves given player skill) plays like a novice when set to low skill but keeps the chess knowledge. Probes for 172 chess concepts stay almost equally accurate across skill settings while move quality changes sharply.
numbers: Retraining only a concept policy head lifts best-move accuracy in the lowest skill band from 14.4% to 82.8% (highest band 89.4% to 91.2%). Blunder rate 52.5% to 8.0%. Sparse-autoencoder steering lifts it from 14.4% to 42.7%.
limits: One chess model; concepts labelled by rules. Recovery is concept-specific; heads trained on one concept lose much of the gain on others.
agent_relevance: Novice-looking output does not mean missing knowledge. Weak output is not proof of weak knowledge, and persona prompts can suppress what the model knows.

source: Gobet et al. (2015) Chunks, Schemata, and Retrieval Structures: Past and Current Computational Models, Frontiers in Psychology 6:1785
finding: Reviews computer models of chunking. CHREST predicted, against the view then, that chess experts should recall random positions better than weaker players, because a model with more chunks is more likely to find chunks by chance. A meta-analysis and Gobet and Waters (2003) supported it, with close agreement to predicted absolute values.
numbers: Saariluoma: experts recalled game positions at over 80%, random at no more than 60%. Gobet (2000) LT-WM implementation gave recall from 10% to 100% for both game and random positions depending on parameters.
limits: Secondary review by the model's own authors. Vicente and Wang (1998) argued standard random positions keep constraints (one white king, at most eight black pawns); CHREST predicted a smaller but real skill effect for fully random positions, and Gobet and Waters found it.
agent_relevance: Chunking is a computational mechanism that makes testable predictions. The surviving version says expertise is a large library of small patterns, which supports retrieval of stored cases over verbal rules.

source: Gobet et al. (2015) Chunks, Schemata, and Retrieval Structures: Past and Current Computational Models, Frontiers in Psychology 6:1785
finding: EPAM-IV models digit-span expertise with a retrieval structure of digits, chunks, super-groups and super-group clusters. CHREST simulated a master memorizing several boards at once with a list of world champions as the retrieval structure.
numbers: Richman et al. (1995) simulated a person memorizing up to 106 digits dictated one per second.
limits: Models from before 2015; none LLM based.
agent_relevance: A retrieval structure is a fixed index into memory, like an agent state file with named slots that code, not the model, reads and writes.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study, AAAI
finding: On verbal and spatial n-back tasks, ChatGPT shows a working-memory limit like the human one: sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at n=3. Adding noise lowers capacity. GPT-4 far exceeds other models; the open-source models tested have very low capacity.
numbers: Humans typically drop at n=3 (Jaeggi 2010 and others). Bloomz-7B, ChatGLM-6B, Vicuna-7B and 13B nearly indistinguishable. GPT-4 not tested above n=3 because of cost. Larger grid raised capacity in the spatial task.
limits: Measures n-back (updating), not chunking. Human comparison rests on cited work, not a matched sample.
agent_relevance: An LLM has a working-memory ceiling that falls with interference, so long streams should be compressed into a state record rather than replayed.

source: Borchers et al. (2026) Large Language Models as Students Who Think Aloud: Overly Coherent, Verbose, and Confident
finding: GPT-4.1 continuing a student's think-aloud in chemistry tutoring writes expert-like text: more coherent, wordier and less variable than 630 real learner utterances. Richer prompt context made it worse. It also overestimated whether the student would get the next step right.
numbers: Cosine similarity to human utterance 0.16 (simple context) and 0.19 (extended). Coherence difference beta -0.22 and -0.44 (p<.001). Calibration bias +0.325 and +0.468. AUC 0.528 [0.480, 0.575], near chance. WizardLM-2-7B replicated (bias 0.452 and 0.548).
limits: One domain (stoichiometry), 630 steps. Blame placed on expert-like training data and missing working-memory limits is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: LLMs default to expert-style worked reasoning even when asked to be novices, and cannot predict what a novice finds hard. Do not simulate users without calibration.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of LLMs with Misconceptions
finding: GPT-4 answers grade-school math almost perfectly (94.8%) but is much worse at playing a novice who picks the answer a given misconception would produce. Few-shot examples with the same misconception help; random few-shot examples did worse than zero-shot.
numbers: Best zero-shot prompt: 61.7% for GPT-4 at choosing the incorrect option linked to a misconception. As tutor, GPT-4 finds the right misconception with 91.9% among 4 options but 39.8% when 100 are listed.
limits: Multiple-choice grade-school maths; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Expert-novice asymmetry in models: easy to be right, hard to be wrong in a human way. Real error examples are the useful scaffold when error modelling is needed.

source: Song, Guo, Lin (2026) Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models
finding: Prompting an LLM to act like a novice is unstable: it drifts into expert explanations. The authors instead unlearn knowledge components, then let the model relearn through teaching dialogue. Accuracy and F1 fall steadily as the unlearned share grows.
numbers: Python concept multiple-choice set (about 2,074 questions over 22 knowledge components). Unlearned model about 0.75 at 10% unlearned, below 0.5 from 40%. Base model about 0.85 accuracy and 0.77 F1. Five seeds.
limits: Small domain; novice is a weight-edited model, not a persona prompt. Relearning shown only in simulated dialogue.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts do not remove knowledge. If a naive reader is needed (a clarity test), use a weaker model or stripped context, not a role instruction.

source: Wu, Alaniz, Schulz, Akata (2025) Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
finding: Borrowing the human chunking idea (cites Chase and Simon 1973 and Miller 1956), the authors extract a dictionary of recurring activity patterns from RNNs trained on sequences with planted regularities, then from LLaMA3-8B. Chunks line up with concepts and part-of-speech tags; grafting a chunk into hidden state changes generated text.
numbers: RNN decoding on simple planted structure reached perfect test decoding; LLaMA3-8B analysed layer by layer on a short text (Emma).
limits: Proof of concept on small data; interpretation is correlational. Not a test of expert memory.
agent_relevance: Chunking is used as an interpretability tool inside LLMs, a possible route to read what a model stores as units. Not yet an agent-loop method.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Concept-Guided Interpretability via Neural Chunking
finding: Extends the above with three chunk extraction methods (discrete sequence chunking, population averaging, unsupervised discovery) and a Reflection Hypothesis that network activity mirrors data regularities. Grafting extracted chunks steers LLaMA-3 output and helps RNNs transfer to new sequences.
numbers: Tested on RNNs and LLaMA3-8B, including question-type classes (ABBR, DESC, ENTY, HUM, LOC, NUM) with chunk decoding percentages per class.
limits: Percentages are class- and layer-specific; steering judged on a small corpus.
agent_relevance: If chunks can be read and steered, an agent might one day check what a model retrieved. Today it is research, not a scaffold step.

source: Zhong, Sivan, Can, Katkov, Tsodyks (2026) Semantic Chunking and the Entropy of Natural Language
finding: LLMs recursively cut text into semantic chunks, forming a tree whose branching predicts an entropy rate close to the LLM-measured one; simpler texts have lower branching.
numbers: Abstract only: children's stories show lower branching and lower entropy than fiction and poetry.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Chunk here means semantic segment, not an expert memory unit.
agent_relevance: LLMs can segment text into meaning units reliably enough to measure; supports chunking long inputs into a tree in code before the model reads them.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Maps LLM agents onto Soar-style cognitive architectures: working memory plus procedural, semantic and episodic long-term memory, with a decision loop of retrieval, reasoning and learning. Soar can write new productions into procedural memory (its chunking) and creates a subgoal at an impasse.
numbers: Soar productions fire by matching working memory; no match or a tie gives an impasse and a subgoal.
limits: Conceptual framework with no benchmark numbers of its own.
agent_relevance: The lineage from Chase-Simon chunking through Soar to agent design. Soar's impasse rule matches guardrail G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Voyager stores each verified action program in a skill library indexed by an embedding of its description, then retrieves skills for new tasks. Like an expert's growing store of chunks, solved sub-problems become reusable units.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x baselines; wooden, stone, iron levels 15.3x, 8.5x, 6.4x faster; only agent to reach diamond. Zero-shot new tasks in a new world: Voyager 3/3 on four tasks (about 18 to 21 iterations) versus 0/3 for ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT.
limits: Minecraft with GPT-4; verification uses environment feedback. Without the library Voyager is slower and less reliable (2/3 on diamond pickaxe, 36 iterations).
agent_relevance: Closest working chunk library in an LLM loop. Admit a skill only after a check passes (G3). Giving the library to AutoGPT also helped (1/3 on three tasks versus 0/3).

source: Ciancarini and Pareschi (2026) What Counts as Strategic Reasoning? A Systematic Mapping of Chess Research on Humans, Engines, and Language Models
finding: Maps 84 core study families on chess across humans, engines, neural systems, LLMs and hybrids. LLM work centres on state representation and generalization; planning, explanation and metacognition are less studied. It credits Chase and Simon for chunking and pattern recognition over larger search.
numbers: 84 core study families.
limits: Abstract and short intro only; no new measurements.
agent_relevance: Consistent with our search: no one has run the classic Chase-Simon recall test on LLMs, so that experiment is open.

source: Bhaskar, Cheng, Chen (2026) Language Models that Play Chess and Explain Their Moves (QUEEN)
finding: A 4B language model joined to a silent expert chess encoder by cross-attention, trained by question answering and iterative distillation, plays at about grandmaster level and explains moves. Pairing an LLM with an expert pattern encoder beats frontier LLMs alone.
numbers: Elo rises by over 900 across seven iterations (1782 to 2697), above frontier models on playing strength and puzzle accuracy, with three orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
limits: Abstract only read. Needs an engine-based expert encoder.
agent_relevance: The expert pattern system sees; the language model explains. Matches our split: code or specialist checks, the model fills the slot.

source: Chase and Simon (1973) Perception in chess (as cited by Pleiss 2026, Wu 2025, Ciancarini and Pareschi 2026)
finding: Founding chunk study: masters recalled game positions far better than novices but not random positions; the gap is explained by more and larger chunks, not larger span. Three 2025-2026 machine papers use it as the human anchor.
numbers: Not opened by this agent; exact numbers belong to angle A files.
limits: Cited only. None of the papers re-runs the recall task on an LLM.
agent_relevance: A recall of game versus random boards (FEN or ASCII) on LLMs has no published run found here; it is a cheap experiment to propose.

source: Synthesis across Pleiss 2026, Karvonen 2024, Toshniwal 2022 (opened papers)
finding: Common thread across chess LLM studies: performance tracks how much a position looks like training data, and models trained on real games learn state-like internal structure. No study found measures chunk size in LLMs directly.
numbers: Numbers are in earlier lines.
limits: Synthesis by this agent, not a new finding. OpenAlex, arXiv and Semantic Scholar rate limits were hit; 3 of 6 WebSearch calls used.
agent_relevance: Feed real verified cases as input and keep unfamiliar-input handling code-checked.
